impl-4 has the cleanest shape. Filtering sits in #[Scope] model scopes with a match-based sort, and a dedicated form request validates the public filters; it is the only one where array query input does not cause a 500. impl-1 is third. Its component form (with action and method props) and its field-error and flash components are nice. But it adds is_admin to the User fillable list, keeps all query logic inline in the controller, has no ordering on related products and the thinnest tests.

impl-2 is last. It has the same fillable issue and inline queries. It also has a real bug: an unknown sort value applies no ordering at all, which makes pagination order nondeterministic. Its resource-controller docblocks add ceremony.

v.rationale: All four suites pass. impl-4 ranks first. It is the only one that separates transient from permanent failures properly: 5xx responses go back to the queue with increasing backoff, while 4xx responses, missing data and missing orders call fail() immediately. It makes exactly one API call per rate-limited attempt and queues the receipt notification. It also has the strongest queue-aware tests (withFakeQueueInteractions, assertFailed). Its main gaps are no guard against reprocessing an already-processed event, duplicate detection by string-matching 'unique' in the exception message, and an api-group session-auth route. impl-2 is a close second: the idiomatic FormRequest/enum/Resource layer, idempotent markAsPaid, and an admin route that actually works with session auth. It loses ground because the in-job HTTP retry loop multiplies API calls per rate-limit slot, a missing secret lets empty-key signatures through, unknown event types are marked processed silently, and permanent errors are retried six times. impl-3 has sound queue semantics ($tries, backoff, failed()), but it breaks the spec by serving the webhook at /api/webhooks/payments. It also treats every QueryException as a duplicate, and its validation and filtering are thin (inline validate, unvalidated status filter, no pagination). impl-1 is last: no $tries, backoff or failed(), and it catches every Throwable, so there are no queue-level retries. With the default single try, jobs released by RateLimited or WithoutOverlapping silently hit MaxAttemptsExceeded and are left pending instead of failed. In-process HTTP retries bypass the rate limit, and signature checking, validation and the admin filter are all done inline with no FormRequest.

I ran `php artisan test` on all four and every suite passed. I also ran a throwaway probe test against each one, covering blank params, array params, a to-only date, a same-day range and ISO datetimes, then deleted it.

impl-4 is the only one with no crash path and no validation that gets bypassed. It uses validated() data, an enum, Number::currency and clean collection pipelines. Its main weakness is that it aggregates in PHP over every eagerly loaded order, which will not scale for a sales report.

impl-1 has the best architecture:
- a thin invokable controller
- a FormRequest that builds a readonly filters DTO
- #[Scope] attribute scopes, which I confirmed exist in the installed Laravel 13.33
- all aggregation in SQL

But ?country[]=x returns a 500, because the request calls strtoupper on the array before validation runs. Its top customers also carry no email, and blank params return 422 instead of being ignored.

impl-3 aggregates correctly in SQL, but ?status= crashes with a 500 (a ValueError from OrderStatus::from('')). It also puts about 80 lines of duplicated query logic in the controller.

impl-2 is correct in the probes but the least idiomatic:
- it reads raw query() values instead of validated() data
- it uses string constants instead of an enum
- it formats money by hand
- it keeps imperative if-blocks in the controller
- it aggregates everything in memory

Final ranking: impl-4, then impl-1, then impl-3, then impl-2. I weighted the crash bugs in impl-1 and impl-3 more heavily than the scalability problem in impl-4, and impl-1's architecture keeps it above impl-3.

v.rationale:
All four suites pass: impl-1 19 tests, impl-2 22, impl-3 18, impl-4 20. I ran the same throwaway probe in each and deleted it afterwards. Duplicate tag names are handled correctly everywhere because sync dedupes them. All four give an empty slug when the title has no letters or digits (e.g. '!!!').

impl-2 ranks first. It is the most idiomatic modern Laravel of the four: an IndexPostRequest with filter helpers and a bounded per_page, #[ObservedBy], #[Scope] attribute scopes, whereRelation, safe()->except() and Gate::authorize. Its controller is the thinnest, and the slug and published_at rules sit in one place and run on every save. It also has the widest test coverage, including the failure paths.

impl-1 is second. The code is clean and the published_at rule is in the model's saving hook. But the index does not validate its query parameters: an invalid status returns an empty 200, and per_page has no limit, so per_page=-1 returns every row.

impl-3 is third. It meets every requirement but puts the publish logic in the controller twice, assigns fields one by one, validates the index inline and uses odd framework-style migration names.

impl-4 is last. It has a real bug: changing the title leaves the old slug in place. It also reads tags from unvalidated input, keeps the slug and publish logic in the controller, has no return types on controller actions, sets 201 by hand and carries boilerplate docblocks.

bugs: Index query params are never validated (app/Http/Controllers/Api/PostController.php:17-28). Probes: ?per_page=-1, ?tag[]=x and ?status[]=x each return HTTP 500.
per_page has no upper bound (PostController.php:28), so ?per_page=100000 is accepted and a client can pull the whole table in one request.
?status=bogus is silently accepted and returns an empty list instead of a 422.
StorePostRequest.php:25 makes status 'required', so a client must always send a status even though the column defaults to draft. This adds friction to the API contract.
The post_tag migration adds id and timestamps (2026_09_23_070854_create_post_tag_table.php:15-19), but tags() has no withTimestamps(), so those pivot timestamps are always null.
Titles made only of punctuation produce an empty slug ('') and then '-2'. All four implementations share this.
antipatterns: app/Http/Controllers/Controller.php:9 adds the AuthorizesRequests trait back to the base controller and uses $this->authorize(). Laravel 11+ skeletons use Gate::authorize() or the #[Authorize]/can middleware instead.
StorePostRequest.php:25 uses new Enum(...) where Rule::enum() is the current idiom.
PostController.php:38 uses collect($validated)->except('tags')->all() where $request->safe()->except('tags') does the same job.
PostController.php:55-57 keeps the slug-regeneration logic in the controller rather than in the model.
PostResource.php:22 reads $this->tags directly instead of whenLoaded, which invites lazy loading.
PostFactory.php:27 runs a DB query (uniqueSlugFor) inside definition().
strengths: Uses a saving hook in booted() to set published_at, which covers both create and update in one place.
uniqueSlugFor ignores the post's own row when updating, and slug regeneration happens only when the title actually changes.
Relationships carry generics docblocks, and tag syncing is written as a collection map.
Tests cover ownership 403s, slug collisions, tag filtering and pagination meta.

bugs: Titles made only of punctuation get an empty slug (''), and the next one gets '-1'. All implementations share this.
Collision suffixes start at '-1' ('hello-world-1'). This is only a style difference from '-2' and does not affect correctness.
antipatterns: app/Observers/PostObserver.php:11-22 puts slug generation and the defaulting of status inside a saving observer. It works and is attached with #[ObservedBy], but the behaviour is implicit and every save path goes through it.
IndexPostRequest.php:33 returns validated('per_page') ?? 15. The value is a string that relies on loose coercion to the int return type.
Post::syncTagsByName (Post.php:42-48) runs firstOrCreate once per tag inside a loop, which is N queries. This is acceptable at this scale.
strengths: The thinnest controller of the four: an IndexPostRequest with filters()/perPage() helpers, safe()->except('tags'), and $request->enum() for the status filter.
Modern Laravel 12/13 idioms: #[Fillable], #[ObservedBy] and #[Scope] attributes, whereRelation, and eager loading of tags:id,name.
Fillable is limited to title, body and status, so slug, published_at and user_id cannot be mass-assigned.
The policy uses $post->user()->is($user).
Index validation rejects bad status, tag and per_page values (bounded between:1,100) with 422. Probes confirmed no 500s.
The most thorough tests: invalid status on store and update, per_page out of range, pagination meta, preservation of published_at, slug regeneration, and travelTo for ordering.

bugs: Titles made only of punctuation produce an empty slug ('') and then '-2'. All implementations share this.
Store never sets published_at through a model-level path, so any other code path that creates or saves a Post does not apply the publish rule. The rule lives only in the controller.
antipatterns: The migrations are named 0001_01_01_000003..5 (database/migrations/), which mimics the framework's skeleton migrations instead of using timestamped names.
PostController.php:64-81 hand-rolls field-by-field isset() assignment and PostStatus::from() instead of fill($request->safe()) plus the enum cast. The controller carries domain logic.
PostController.php:22-26 uses inline $request->validate in the controller for the index instead of a FormRequest.
Post.php:16 includes 'user_id' in Fillable, even though posts are created through the relation.
The status scope (Post.php:44-47) accepts PostStatus|string and re-parses the value, so the scope does validation work.
PostResource.php:24 reads tags without whenLoaded.
strengths: Validates index filters, including a bounded per_page. Probes showed 422 for bad input and no 500s.
Adds #[Scope] query scopes for status and tag, and puts uniqueSlug on the model with an ignore-self option.
Tests use the expressive assertion helpers (assertCreated, assertForbidden, assertUnprocessable) and cover tag reuse, slug regeneration and preservation of published_at.

bugs: Update sets published_at only when isDirty('status') (PostController.php:74). A post that is already 'published' but has a null published_at, for example after an import, never gets a published_at when it is re-published.
Titles made only of punctuation produce an empty slug ('') and then '-2'. All implementations share this.
The index has no way to control page size and ignores per_page. This is acceptable, but the paginated API is rigid.
antipatterns: The publish rule is duplicated in store (PostController.php:50-52) and update (PostController.php:74-76), and the slug generation (PostController.php:112-124) is a private controller method. This is domain logic in the controller rather than in the model or an observer.
PostController.php:23-26 validates the index inline instead of in a FormRequest.
Stub docblocks restate the method names ('Display a listing...', 'Store a newly created...') throughout the controller and policy.
PostResource.php:23 formats published_at as ISO8601 by hand while created_at and updated_at use the default serialization, so date formats are inconsistent.
The controller methods have no return types.
(new PostResource(...))->response()->setStatusCode(201) is unnecessary, because a resource wrapping a recently created model already returns 201.
strengths: Correct on every core requirement: 401 for guests, 403 for non-owners, unique slugs, tags created on the fly, and filters that return 422 on bad input.
Fillable excludes user_id, and slug and published_at are never taken from request input.
Uses whenLoaded for tags and a composite primary key on the pivot table.
Good test coverage, including preservation of published_at, tag sync replacement, and guest checks on all endpoints.

v.rationale:
All four suites pass: 20, 18, 22 and 19 tests for impl-4, impl-3, impl-2 and impl-1. Sanctum isn't installed, so every implementation uses the 'auth' guard with actingAs, which the task allows.

One probe test was run against each implementation and then deleted. It showed that impl-1 is the only one that returns HTTP 500 for malformed index input (per_page=-1, tag[]=x, status[]=x). impl-1 also leaves per_page unbounded, makes status required on create, and adds the AuthorizesRequests trait back to the base controller. Those real bugs put it last.

impl-2 is the most idiomatic modern Laravel:
- an IndexPostRequest with filter helpers
- a thin controller that uses safe()->except()
- #[ObservedBy] and #[Scope] attributes, and whereRelation
- a tight Fillable list
- the broadest failure-path tests

impl-3 is correct and validates per_page with an upper bound. It loses points for:
- skeleton-style 0001_01_01 migration names
- manual field-by-field assignment in update
- inline validation in the controller
- user_id in Fillable

impl-4 is correct and well tested. However, it duplicates the publish logic across store and update and keeps slug generation in the controller. It also has an isDirty('status') edge case that stops an already-published post with a null published_at from getting one, and it carries stub docblocks throughout.

All four produce an empty slug for titles made only of punctuation.
